chapter_summary:
In most games, the world isn't static. Enemies appear, projectiles are fired, pickups are collected, and effects are triggered. This dynamic creation and removal of game objects is managed through **spawning** and **destroying Actors**. Spawning allows you to instantiate new instances of a Blueprint Class during runtime, bringing them into existence in your game world. Destroying Actors removes them, freeing up memory and resources. Mastering these operations is crucial for building interactive and evolving game environments.

The primary Blueprint node for creating new Actors is **`Spawn Actor from Class`**. This powerful node allows you to specify which Blueprint Class you want to create (e.g., `BP_Projectile`, `BP_Enemy`), and crucially, where and how it should appear in the world. The `Spawn Transform` pin is vital; it takes a `Transform` struct (which includes `Location`, `Rotation`, and `Scale`) to define the initial position, orientation, and size of the new Actor. A common mistake here is to leave the `Spawn Transform` as default (often `0,0,0`), leading to Actors appearing at the world origin, which might not be where you intend. It's good practice to derive the `Spawn Transform` from an existing Actor's location (e.g., a "Spawn Point" Actor, or the muzzle of a weapon) or to construct it dynamically. You can use nodes like `Get Actor Transform`, `Make Transform`, or `Combine Transforms` to precisely control this.

Other important parameters for `Spawn Actor from Class` include `Owner` and `Collision Handling Override`. The `Owner` pin allows you to assign an owning Actor to the newly spawned instance. This is particularly useful for game logic where spawned objects (like projectiles) need to know which player or enemy created them, or for garbage collection purposes. For example, a projectile might need to know its owner to avoid damaging them. The `Collision Handling Override` pin dictates how the spawned Actor handles initial collisions at its spawn location. Options like `Always Spawn, Ignore Collisions` or `Try To Adjust Location But Always Spawn` give you control over whether the Actor should appear even if its spawn location is already occupied, or if it should attempt to find a clear spot. For instance, if you're spawning multiple enemies in a small area, you might want them to adjust their positions slightly to avoid spawning directly inside each other.

Once an Actor has served its purpose, it's good practice to remove it from the game world using the **`Destroy Actor`** node. This frees up memory and processing power that the Actor was consuming. For example, a projectile should destroy itself after hitting something or after a certain amount of time. A pickup item should destroy itself once collected. However, destroying Actors isn't without its caveats. A critical safety note: if other Blueprints still hold a reference to a destroyed Actor, attempting to access properties or call functions on that reference will result in errors, crashes, or unpredictable behavior (often referred to as "dangling pointers" or "pending kill" references). It's essential to ensure that any references to an Actor are cleared or handled gracefully before or immediately after it's destroyed. For instance, if a player's HUD has a reference to a specific `HealthPack` Actor, that reference should be set to `None` or validated before use once the `HealthPack` is picked up and destroyed.

While `Spawn Actor from Class` and `Destroy Actor` are your primary tools, you might sometimes need to find existing Actors in the world. Nodes like `Get All Actors Of Class` or `Get All Actors With Tag` can retrieve references to all Actors of a certain type or with a specific tag. While useful for debugging or specific scenarios, these nodes can be computationally expensive if used frequently, especially with many Actors. It's generally better to establish references at `BeginPlay` or through Event Dispatchers if possible, rather than constantly searching the entire world. Building progressively, you'll find that managing Actor lifecycles effectively is key to a stable and performant game.

screens.title: Spawning and Destroying Actors
screens.subtitle: Dynamically create, configure, and remove Actor instances safely at runtime

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how to bring Actors into the world at runtime and remove them cleanly when they are no longer needed. Spawning is the act of instantiating an Actor Blueprint Class so it can participate in gameplay: enemies, projectiles, pickups, and effects. Destroying is the complementary operation that frees memory and stops processing when an Actor has served its purpose. Getting both right matters for correctness and performance. You will see how to use the Spawn Actor from Class node, how to build a correct Spawn Transform, why assigning an Owner can simplify game logic, and how Collision Handling Override affects whether an Actor appears if the spawn location is occupied. We also cover Destroy Actor and the danger of dangling references so your Blueprints do not try to access objects that no longer exist. Practical examples include making a projectile Blueprint that self-destructs on impact or after a timer, and wiring a character input to spawn that projectile with the correct transform and owner. By the end you will be able to spawn and cleanly remove Actors while avoiding common errors and keeping your game stable.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Dynamic Actor lifecycle management lets your game world change during play. Correct spawning, ownership, and destruction keep gameplay predictable and performant.

Spawning and Destroying Actors

Understand how to create Actors at runtime, configure their initial transform and ownership, and remove them safely to keep gameplay stable.

How to use Spawn Actor from Class, build spawn transforms, assign owners, and destroy Actors safely.

Outcome

You will implement a projectile that spawns from the player and self-destructs on impact or after a timeout.

Chapter orientation

Spawning and destruction are the runtime lifecycle operations for Actors. Treat them as paired actions: how you bring an Actor into the world determines how you should manage references and teardown later.

Second, you'll learn how to use the Spawn Actor from Class node to create Blueprints at a specified transform and orientation, including practical examples like firing a projectile. Third, you will configure important spawn options such as the Spawn Transform, Owner assignment, and Collision Handling Override so newly spawned Actors behave predictably. Fourth, you'll implement the Destroy Actor node to safely remove Actors, and you will learn to handle references and avoid invalid access. Each objective includes practical reasons and a small mnemonic so the skill is actionable. These objectives ensure you can both implement and reason about dynamic Actor lifecycles in a stable way.

screens.title: What is spawning?
screens.subtitle: Definition, purpose, and a gameplay metaphor

narration.text: Spawning is the runtime creation of an Actor instance from a Blueprint Class so it can participate in gameplay immediately. Think of a spawned Actor as a fresh object that did not exist in the level at design time but is created by your logic at runtime. This includes bullets fired by a player, enemies that appear during a wave, timed pickups, or visual effects created on demand. A clear example: when the player presses fire you spawn a BP_Projectile and set its initial velocity; that projectile is now an independent Actor that moves, collides, and eventually destroys itself. Spawning matters because it lets designers and programmers build dynamic, responsive worlds without placing every object by hand. A common misconception is that spawn is only for simple things — in fact, anything that can be an Actor can be spawned and should be treated as a proper instance with its own lifecycle and memory footprint. Another pitfall is leaving the spawn transform unset; if you pass a default Transform the Actor commonly appears at world origin, causing invisible collisions or lost projectiles. Remember: spawning creates an independent lifecycle. Ask yourself: who owns this instance, and how will it be cleaned up when done?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Spawning creates an Actor instance at runtime so it participates in physics, rendering, and logic immediately.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What is spawning?
Core Concept

Spawning explained

Create instances of Blueprint Classes during gameplay so they act like normal Actors.

Why spawn?
  • Enable dynamic gameplay: enemies, projectiles, pickups appear when needed.
  • Save design time by not pre-placing every instance in the level.
  • Control lifecycle and memory usage by destroying when finished.
Concrete example

Pressing Fire spawns BP_Projectile with a muzzle transform and Owner set to the player so it doesn't damage its creator.

Common mistake

Leaving the Spawn Transform default causes Actors to appear at world origin; always derive transforms from a spawn point or socket.

Analogy

Think of spawning as printing a new game object from a template. The template is the Blueprint class and the printed copy is a live Actor that can be manipulated independently.

Key Takeaway

Treat every spawned Actor as a distinct object with its own lifecycle and clean it up when finished.

screens.title: Spawn Actor from Class node
screens.subtitle: Parameters, Owner, and Collision Handling options

narration.text: The Spawn Actor from Class node is your primary tool for creating Actor instances at runtime. It requires a Class to instantiate and a Spawn Transform that defines Location, Rotation, and Scale. Optional pins include Owner and Collision Handling Override. Owner links the spawned Actor to another Actor for gameplay logic or replication; for example, a projectile that was spawned by a player should have that player as Owner so it can exclude the creator from damage checks. Collision Handling Override controls whether the engine forces the new instance into the world even if the spawn location is occupied. Options include Always Spawn, Ignore Collisions, or Try To Adjust Location But Always Spawn. Use 'Try To Adjust' when you need the Actor but want it nudged to a valid spot. Always Spawn, Ignore Collisions is useful for visual effects that can overlap. A practical pattern is to compute a precise spawn transform using a socket or a spawn point Actor and connect Self to Owner from the spawning Blueprint. A common misconception is that Owner is only for replication; it also helps game logic, such as damage attribution and cleanup paths. Finally, be mindful that spawning many heavy Actors without pooling can be expensive, so reserve spawn frequency for necessary cases.

keyIdea.title: Spawn node essentials
keyIdea.text: Always provide a correct Spawn Transform and consider Owner and Collision Handling to control initial behavior of the new Actor.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Spawn Actor from Class
Process Flow

Using the Spawn node

Pick a class, compute a spawn transform, set Owner and collision handling, then execute the node.

Step 1 — Choose Class

Select the Blueprint Class to instantiate, e.g., BP_Projectile or BP_Enemy.

Step 2 — Build Spawn Transform

Use Get Actor Transform, socket transforms, or Make Transform to provide Location, Rotation, and Scale.

Step 3 — Set Owner & Collision

Connect Self to Owner to track creation and choose Collision Handling to control initial placement behavior.

Collision Handling examples
  • Always Spawn, Ignore Collisions: good for VFX that can overlap.
  • Try To Adjust Location But Always Spawn: nudges spawn location to avoid overlaps for NPCs.
  • Do Not Spawn If Colliding: safe when placement must be exact.
Misconception

Owner is not only for replication — it also communicates creation intent and is used by logic like damage filtering.

Key Takeaway

Provide a correct transform and owner; choose collision handling based on gameplay needs.

screens.title: Constructing a Spawn Transform
screens.subtitle: Get Actor Transform, sockets, and Make Transform patterns

narration.text: A correct Spawn Transform is the most common source of spawning bugs. The Transform contains Location, Rotation, and Scale. You often derive it from an existing Actor or a socket: for example, use Get Socket Transform on a weapon mesh with a 'Muzzle' socket to ensure the projectile starts at the muzzle and inherits the correct orientation. If a socket is not available, compute a point in front of the character by adding Get Actor Forward Vector multiplied by a distance to Get Actor Location. Another option is to use Make Transform and pass explicit values. A compact pseudocode example helps illustrate the pattern: compute location from owner location plus forward offset, compute rotation from the owner's control or socket, then call Spawn Actor from Class with this Transform and set Owner to Self. Avoid leaving the Transform unset — that places the Actor at world origin. A misconception is to assume scale is irrelevant; some Blueprints use scale to size collision or visuals, so set it intentionally. When spawning many projectiles per second, building transforms with simple vector math is lightweight and reliable. Finally, validate the spawn location if necessary, and consider Collision Handling Override if the location might be occupied.

keyIdea.title: Spawn Transform tip
keyIdea.text: Use sockets or compute a forward offset from the spawner to avoid origin spawns; set rotation so physics and movement start correctly.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Constructing a Spawn Transform
Blueprint pattern

Build reliable transforms

Use socket transforms or compute relative offsets from the owner to avoid origin spawns and wrong rotations.

When to use sockets

If your mesh has a Muzzle socket, Get Socket Transform ensures precise placement and orientation for projectiles.

When to compute offset

If sockets aren't present, calculate location using Get Actor Location + Get Actor Forward Vector * distance.

Blueprint-like pseudocode
// Compute spawn transform for projectile
Vector ownerLocation = GetActorLocation(Self)
Vector forward = GetActorForwardVector(Self)
Vector spawnLocation = ownerLocation + forward * 100
Rotator spawnRotation = GetControlRotation(Self) // or GetActorRotation
Transform spawnTransform = MakeTransform(spawnLocation, spawnRotation, Vector(1,1,1))
SpawnActorFromClass(BP_Projectile, spawnTransform, Owner=Self, CollisionHandling=TryToAdjust)
Key Takeaway

Never rely on default transform; always compute or read a specific transform for predictable spawn results.

screens.title: Owner and collision handling
screens.subtitle: How Owner affects logic and collision override choices

narration.text: Owner and Collision Handling Override are two small parameters that have big effects on runtime behavior. Owner sets which Actor is considered the creator of the new instance. This matters for gameplay, for example when projectiles must not damage their originator or when cleanup policies depend on ownership. Use Owner to make attribution and filtering simple: the spawned object can query its Owner to implement friendly-fire checks or scoring attribution. Collision Handling Override determines how the engine treats an occupied spawn location. If you select Always Spawn, Ignore Collisions, the Actor is created even if it overlaps others — useful for cosmetic effects. Try To Adjust Location will attempt to find a nearby free spot and still spawn, which is useful for NPCs to avoid overlapping each other. A common misconception is that ignoring collisions is always safe; overlapping physics bodies can cause immediate penetration or jitter. When precision matters, prefer computing a valid transform and using Try To Adjust or blocking spawn to ensure correct placement. In networked games, ownership also affects replication and authority logic, so be intentional when assigning it.

keyIdea.title: Practical rule
keyIdea.text: Assign Owner for attribution and choose collision handling based on whether visual overlap or physical accuracy matters.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Owner & Collision Handling
Definition

Owner and collision behavior

Owner ties a spawned Actor to its creator. Collision handling defines how to place the new Actor if the spawn point is occupied.

Owner uses
  • Damage attribution and friendly-fire checks.
  • Cleanup policies and ownership-based permissions.
  • Replication logic in networked games.
Collision handling choices

Pick Ignore Collisions for VFX, Try To Adjust for NPC placement, or Block spawn when exact placement is required.

Concrete scenario

Spawn a projectile with Owner set to the player. The projectile checks Owner to avoid damaging its creator. Use Try To Adjust for enemy spawn points in crowded waves to prevent overlap.

Pitfall

Ignoring collisions for physical Actors can cause immediate penetration or unexpected physics. Choose the override based on whether the Actor needs valid collision state on spawn.

Key Takeaway

Assign Owner for clear logic and pick collision handling to match gameplay reliability vs. cosmetic behavior.

screens.title: Destroy Actor safely
screens.subtitle: Teardown patterns, clearing references, and the IsValid check

narration.text: Destroy Actor removes an Actor instance from the game world and frees its resources. Use it when an Actor has completed its purpose, such as a projectile after hitting a surface or a pickup after being collected. The critical safety concern is references: other Blueprints might still hold pointers to the Actor you just destroyed. If they try to access properties or call functions on a destroyed Actor you will see invalid behavior or runtime errors. To avoid this, clear references explicitly or guard accesses with an IsValid node before operating on a reference. A common pattern for projectiles is to call Destroy Actor on Self when a hit is detected or when a timer elapses; any systems that tracked that projectile should listen for an event or validate the reference before use. Another pattern is to set a pointer to None from the owning object when it is destroyed. Remember that destruction is not always instantaneous in the editor's internals; use IsValid checks rather than assuming a pointer is immediately nullified elsewhere. Misconception: Destroying an Actor automatically clears every reference across Blueprints — it does not. Be explicit and defensive when managing references.

keyIdea.title: Safety first
keyIdea.text: Always clear or validate references to an Actor before or after destroying it to avoid invalid access.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Destroy Actor safely
Definition

Destroy Actor

Remove an Actor from the world and free associated processing. Use it when an object is consumed or no longer needed.

Common uses
  • Projectiles on hit or after timeout.
  • Pickups when collected.
  • Temporary visual effects after their lifetime.
Dangling reference pitfall

Other Blueprints may still hold references. Clear or validate these references to avoid invalid access errors.

Safe teardown pattern
  1. Notify interested systems (event or dispatcher).
  2. Clear references on owners or trackers.
  3. Call Destroy Actor on the target.
Key Takeaway

Destruction must be paired with reference management; validate before use and clear pointers when appropriate.

screens.title: Build BP_Projectile
screens.subtitle: Components, timers, and On Component Hit teardown

narration.text: Let's build a BP_Projectile step by step. Start with an Actor Blueprint named BP_Projectile. Add a Sphere Collision component with a small radius (for example radius ten) and set its Collision Presets to Projectile. Add a Static Mesh as a child for visuals and add a Projectile Movement component configured with an Initial Speed and Max Speed of two thousand. In the Event Graph, implement Event BeginPlay to start a Set Timer by Event for three seconds that calls a DestroySelf custom event when the timer completes. For collisions, add an On Component Hit event on the Sphere Collision and connect it to Destroy Actor on Self. Optionally spawn an emitter at the hit location before destroying for feedback. This pattern ensures the projectile destroys itself either on impact or after a timeout. A common misconception is to rely only on collisions to clean up projectiles; a backup timer prevents stuck projectiles from lingering forever. When testing, verify that collision presets and generate overlap events are correctly set so hits register reliably. Build BP_Projectile means use a collision component, projectile movement, an impact handler, and a self-destruct timer to reliably clean up projectiles.. In practical terms, components, timers, and on component hit teardown. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Projectile pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a collision component, projectile movement, an impact handler, and a self-destruct timer to reliably clean up projectiles.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Build BP_Projectile
Hands-on

Projectile Blueprint

Components, events, and a self-destruct timer form a reliable projectile implementation.

Components to add
  • Sphere Collision (radius ~10), Collision Presets = Projectile, Generate Overlap Events checked.
  • Static Mesh (Shape_Sphere) as a child.
  • Projectile Movement with Initial and Max Speed = 2000.
Event Graph

BeginPlay: Set Timer by Event, Time = 3.0, calls DestroySelf. On Component Hit: Destroy Actor Self.

Event Graph pseudocode
Event BeginPlay:
  Set Timer by Event (Time=3.0, Looping=false)
    -> Custom Event DestroySelf

On Component Hit (Sphere Collision):
  Spawn Emitter at Location (optional)
  Destroy Actor (Target=Self)

Custom Event DestroySelf:
  Destroy Actor (Target=Self)
Key Takeaway

Combine collision and a timer for robust tear down so projectiles cannot persist indefinitely.

screens.title: Implement Player Spawning
screens.subtitle: InputAction Fire, socket transforms, and Owner wiring

narration.text: Wiring player input to spawn projectiles ties together the earlier concepts. First, add an Input Action named Fire and map it to a mouse button. In your character Blueprint, add the Input Action Fire (Pressed) event. From the Pressed pin, create a Spawn Actor from Class node and set the Class to BP_Projectile. For Spawn Transform, prefer Get Socket Transform on the character mesh using a 'Muzzle' socket or compute spawnLocation = GetActorLocation + GetActorForwardVector * 100 for a forward offset. Connect Self to the Owner pin so the projectile knows who created it. Optionally set Collision Handling Override to Try To Adjust Location But Always Spawn if you expect crowded spawn points. Test by playing, firing, and watching the projectile travel and destroy itself on hit or after the timer. A common trap is to use screen-space or camera location for spawn without converting to world-space, which places projectiles in the wrong spot. Validate that the Owner is set and that collisions register; use print statements or visual emitters if you need to debug spawn orientation. This wiring produces tight, predictable firing behavior.

keyIdea.title: Player spawn wiring
keyIdea.text: Use Input Action Fire to call Spawn Actor with a socket-based or computed transform, and set Owner to the character.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Implement Player Spawning
Live coding

Player spawn wiring

Map input to Spawn Actor from Class, supply a correct transform, and set Owner to Self.

Practical steps
  1. Add Input Action Fire in Project Settings and map to Left Mouse Button.
  2. In ThirdPersonCharacter Blueprint, add Input Action Fire (Pressed).
  3. Spawn BP_Projectile with Spawn Transform from a socket or forward offset; set Owner to Self.
Spawn wiring pseudocode
On Input Action Fire (Pressed):
  Transform muzzleTransform = GetSocketTransform(Mesh, 'Muzzle')
  // or compute using GetActorLocation + ForwardVector * 100
  SpawnActorFromClass(BP_Projectile, muzzleTransform, Owner=Self, CollisionHandling=TryToAdjust)
Key Takeaway

Use sockets for precision and assign Owner so the projectile knows its creator and behaves accordingly.

screens.title: Finding Actors vs direct references
screens.subtitle: Get All Actors nodes and performance trade-offs

narration.text: Nodes like Get All Actors Of Class or Get All Actors With Tag let you find Actor instances dynamically, which can be useful for quick prototyping or single-shot logic. For example, in a level with a single BP_EnemySpawnPoint you can use Get All Actors Of Class and then Get Actor Transform to feed the spawn node. However, these nodes iterate across the world and become expensive if called frequently, especially with large numbers of Actors. A better pattern is to store references at BeginPlay, pass references through level setup, or use Event Dispatchers to notify systems of relevant Actors. Consider using tags sparingly and caching results rather than calling global searches every frame. A common misconception is that Get All Actors is cheap; it is appropriate for initialization or debugging but not for per-frame or high-frequency spawning logic. For spawn points, keep a reference to the specific Actor you intend to use and use Get Actor Transform on that reference. This keeps spawning deterministic and efficient, and simplifies ownership wiring because you already have a reference to set as Owner if appropriate.

keyIdea.title: Caching is better
keyIdea.text: Use Get All Actors sparingly. Cache or pass references for frequent spawn operations to avoid performance hits.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Finding Actors vs References
Comparison

Get All Actors vs Direct References

Choose initialization-time retrieval or cached references over frequent global searches.

When Get All Actors is OK

Level setup, one-off scripts, or debugging where performance is not critical.

When to avoid it

High-frequency logic like spawning many projectiles or per-frame checks; prefer cached references or dispatcher events.

Practical pattern

At BeginPlay, find required actors once and store their references. Use those stored references for future spawning and Owner assignment.

Key Takeaway

Prefer references established at BeginPlay or via dispatchers over repeated Get All Actors calls.

screens.title: Testing and debugging spawns
screens.subtitle: Validate transforms, collisions, and reference lifecycles

narration.text: Testing spawning and destruction requires a checklist approach. First, verify the Spawn Transform: use debug prints or temporary visual markers to show the Location and Rotation used by the Spawn node. Confirm sockets exist and that forward offsets are converted to world space. Second, check collision: test each Collision Handling Override option to see whether actors overlap or get adjusted as you expect. Third, observe Owner wiring by confirming the spawned Actor can reference its Owner and behave accordingly — for example, ensure a projectile ignores its Owner when applying damage. Fourth, validate destruction paths: when a projectile is destroyed, ensure other systems do not retain invalid references. Add IsValid guards before accessing references and clear pointers in owner or manager Blueprints. Finally, measure performance: spawning many heavy Actors can be costly, so profile or test with representative numbers. A common debugging trick is to temporarily spawn a simple debug mesh instead of the full Blueprint to isolate transform and collision issues before integrating complex components. This systematic process reduces surprises during runtime. Testing and debugging spawns means debug transforms, collision handling, owner behavior, and reference cleanup systematically to ensure reliable spawn/destruction workflows.. In practical terms, validate transforms, collisions, and reference lifecycles. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Testing checklist
keyIdea.text: Debug transforms, collision handling, owner behavior, and reference cleanup systematically to ensure reliable spawn/destruction workflows.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Testing and debugging spawns

Debug checklist

  • Print or visualize the Spawn Transform values to confirm placement and rotation.
  • Test Collision Handling Override options and watch for overlap behavior.
  • Verify Owner references by checking that the spawned Actor can access Owner properties safely.
  • Ensure Destroy Actor paths clear references or use IsValid before access.
  • Profile spawn frequency for performance; consider pooling for heavy objects.
Quick debugging trick

Spawn a simple debug mesh or particle instead of the full Blueprint to isolate transform and collision issues before adding movement or complex components.

Key Takeaway

Validate placement, collision behavior, ownership, and reference cleanup using a consistent checklist.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Quickly review the essential terms you used in this chapter. Spawning is the runtime creation of Actor instances from Blueprint Classes. Destroying is the removal of those Actors when they are no longer needed. The Spawn Actor from Class node performs the instantiation and accepts a Spawn Transform, Owner, and Collision Handling Override. The Spawn Transform is the Location, Rotation, and Scale that determines where and how the Actor appears. Owner links the spawned instance to a creator for logic and replication. Collision Handling Override dictates how to treat an occupied spawn location. Finally, dangling references occur when other Blueprints hold pointers to destroyed Actors; guard accesses with IsValid and clear references after destruction. Hold these concepts in mind as you implement projectiles and other dynamic objects so creation and cleanup remain predictable and safe.

keyIdea.title: Memory aid

Spawning

Summary

Always supply a correct transform and owner when spawning, and clear or validate references when destroying to maintain stable gameplay.

narration.text: Keep these short definitions handy as you work. Owner: the Actor that created or owns a spawned instance; use it to attribute actions or filter collisions. Collision Handling Override: spawn-time option that controls whether to force spawn, ignore collisions, or attempt to adjust the location. Dangling Reference: a pointer to an Actor that has been destroyed; always validate references or clear them to prevent invalid access. These concepts repeatedly appear in spawning workflows. Before you ship, test creation and destruction together to verify that owners, collisions, and references behave as intended. A quick mental checklist: transform correct, owner assigned, collision policy chosen, references cleared. That checklist will prevent most common issues when working with dynamic Actors. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
